## Proof

**Yes**, such an uncountable set $T$ exists.

**Construction.** Since the rationals $\mathbb{Q}$ are countable, fix a bijection $f\colon \mathbb{N}^+\to \mathbb{Q}$. For each real number $r\in\mathbb{R}$, define
$$C_r \;=\; \{\,n\in\mathbb{N}^+ : f(n) < r\,\}\;\subseteq\;\mathbb{N}^+.$$
Set $T = \{\,C_r : r\in\mathbb{R}\,\}$.

**$T$ is a chain.** Take any two members $C_r, C_s\in T$. Either $r\le s$ or $s\le r$. If $r\le s$, then $f(n)<r\Rightarrow f(n)<s$, so $C_r\subseteq C_s$. Likewise, if $s\le r$, then $C_s\subseteq C_r$. Hence every pair in $T$ is comparable under inclusion.

**$T$ is uncountable.** It suffices to show the map $r\mapsto C_r$ is injective. Let $r<s$ be two distinct reals. By density of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$, choose a rational $q$ with $r\le q<s$. Let $n=f^{-1}(q)$. Then $f(n)=q<s$, so $n\in C_s$; but $f(n)=q\ge r$, so $n\notin C_r$. Thus $C_r\subsetneq C_s$, and in particular $C_r\ne C_s$. Therefore $r\mapsto C_r$ is injective, $|T|=|\mathbb{R}|$, and $T$ is uncountable.

**Conclusion.** $T$ is an uncountable family of subsets of $\mathbb{N}^+$ totally ordered by inclusion, as required. $\blacksquare$
